prompt: A pro athlete played for $17$ years and earned $72$ million dollars. She was paid $k$ million dollars a year, where $k$ is an integer, and received an extra one million dollars each year that her team made the playoffs. Compute the number of years her team made the playoffs.

solutions.title: Set up an equation
solutions.body:
If the team made the playoffs in $n$ of the $17$ years, then $17k+n=72$ with $0\le n\le17$. So $72-n$ is a multiple of $17$ between $55$ and $72$: only $68$, giving $n=4$ (and $k=4$).

**Answer: 4**

prompt: In circle $O$, $\overline{PO}\perp\overline{OB}$, and $PO$ equals the length of the diameter of circle $O$. Segment $PB$ meets the circle again at $A$. Compute $\dfrac{PA}{AB}$.

solutions.title: Power of a point
solutions.body:
Let the radius be $r$. Then $PO=2r$, $OB=r$, so $PB=\sqrt{4r^2+r^2}=r\sqrt5$. The line $PO$ meets the circle at distances $r$ and $3r$ from $P$ (at $2r-r$ and $2r+r$), so the power of $P$ is $r\cdot3r=3r^2=PA\cdot PB$. Thus $PA=\frac{3r^2}{r\sqrt5}=\frac{3r}{\sqrt5}$ and $AB=r\sqrt5-\frac{3r}{\sqrt5}=\frac{2r}{\sqrt5}$.

$\frac{PA}{AB}=\frac32$.

**Answer: $\frac32$**

prompt: If $a$ and $b$ are the roots of $11x^2-4x-2=0$, compute the product $$\left(1+a+a^2+a^3+\cdots\right)\left(1+b+b^2+b^3+\cdots\right).$$

solutions.title: Geometric series
solutions.body:
The roots are $\frac{4\pm\sqrt{104}}{22}$, both between $-1$ and $1$, so the series converge to $\frac1{1-a}$ and $\frac1{1-b}$. Their product is $\frac1{(1-a)(1-b)}=\frac1{1-(a+b)+ab}$. By Vieta, $a+b=\frac4{11}$ and $ab=-\frac2{11}$, so the product is $\frac1{1-\frac4{11}-\frac2{11}}=\frac{11}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{11}{5}$**

prompt: The measure of $\angle PAQ$ is $60^\circ$, ray $\overrightarrow{AB}$ bisects $\angle PAQ$, and circles $P$ and $Q$ (centred at $P$ and $Q$, with radii $1$ and $2$ respectively) are tangent to $\overrightarrow{AB}$. Compute the distance from $P$ to $Q$.

solutions.title: Two $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles
solutions.body:
The bisector makes $30^\circ$ with $AP$ and with $AQ$. The distance from $P$ to the line $AB$ is the radius $1$, so $AP=\frac{1}{\sin30^\circ}=2$; likewise $AQ=\frac{2}{\sin30^\circ}=4$.

In $\triangle PAQ$, $AP=2$, $AQ=4$ and $\angle PAQ=60^\circ$, so by the law of cosines $PQ^2=4+16-2\cdot2\cdot4\cos60^\circ=12$ and $PQ=2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

prompt: If $\dfrac{\log_b a}{\log_c a}=\dfrac{19}{99}$, then $\dfrac bc=c^k$. Compute $k$.

solutions.title: Change of base
solutions.body:
$\frac{\log_ba}{\log_ca}=\frac{\ln a/\ln b}{\ln a/\ln c}=\frac{\ln c}{\ln b}=\frac{19}{99}$, so $\ln b=\frac{99}{19}\ln c$, i.e. $b=c^{99/19}$. Then $\frac bc=c^{99/19-1}=c^{80/19}$, so $k=\frac{80}{19}$.

**Answer: $\frac{80}{19}$**

prompt: Let $A_0A_1\cdots A_{11}$ be a regular $12$-sided polygon whose area is $24$. Form convex polygons by first connecting consecutive vertices, then joining the first and the last vertices. For example, polygons $A_3A_4A_5A_6$ or $A_{10}A_{11}A_0A_1A_2A_3A_4$, as well as the entire $12$-gon can be formed. Compute the sum of the areas of all the distinct polygons that can be formed.

solutions.title: Pair each polygon with its complement
solutions.body:
A polygon is determined by a chord $A_iA_j$: it is the polygon on one side of the chord, using consecutive vertices. The chord $A_iA_j$ gives two polygons (the two sides), whose areas add up to the area $24$ of the $12$-gon.

There are $\binom{12}2=66$ chords. Of these, $12$ are sides of the $12$-gon, and these produce only the whole $12$-gon (and a degenerate segment), so count the whole $12$-gon once. The other $54$ chords each give a pair of polygons of total area $24$.

Total: $54\cdot24+24=55\cdot24=1320$.

**Answer: 1320**

prompt: Arrange the following products in increasing order from left to right: $$1000!,\quad(400!)(400!)(200!),\quad(500!)(500!),\quad(600!)(300!)(100!),\quad(700!)(300!).$$

solutions.title: Compare in steps
solutions.body:
- $1000!>700!\,300!$, since $\binom{1000}{300}>1$.
- $700!\,300!>500!\,500!$: $\frac{1000!}{700!300!}=\binom{1000}{300}<\binom{1000}{500}=\frac{1000!}{500!500!}$, because the central binomial coefficient is the largest.
- $500!\,500!>600!\,300!\,100!$: $\dfrac{500!\,500!}{600!\,300!\,100!}=\dfrac{(500\cdots401)(400\cdots301)}{(600\cdots501)(100\cdots1)}$. Termwise, $\frac{500-i}{600-i}\ge\frac45$ and $\frac{400-i}{100-i}\ge3$ ($0\le i\le99$), so the ratio is at least $\left(\frac45\cdot3\right)^{100}=\left(\frac{12}5\right)^{100}>1$.
- $600!\,300!\,100!>400!\,400!\,200!$: divide both by $400!\,300!\,100!$ to get $600\cdot599\cdots401$ versus $(400\cdots301)(200\cdots101)$. Both are products of $200$ factors, and sorting the factors, each factor of the left product is larger than the corresponding factor of the right product.

**Answer: $400!\,400!\,200!<600!\,300!\,100!<500!\,500!<700!\,300!<1000!$**

prompt: Two congruent rectangles are positioned in a right triangle of legs $a$ and $b$ as shown. Both rectangles have a vertex on the hypotenuse and a long side on a leg. If $a$ and $b$ can vary and the short side of each rectangle is $kb$ for a real number $k$, compute the largest possible value for $k$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put the right angle at the origin with legs on the axes, hypotenuse $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$. The lower rectangle has height $kb$, so its upper right vertex is on the hypotenuse at $x=a(1-k)$; its long side is $L=a(1-k)$. The upper rectangle has width $kb$, so its upper right vertex is at $y=b\left(1-\frac{kb}a\right)$ and it sits on top of the lower one, so its long side is $L=b\left(1-\frac{kb}a\right)-kb$.

Equating: $a-ak=b-\frac{kb^2}a-kb$, so $k\,(a^2-b^2-ab)=a^2-ab$, i.e. $k=\dfrac{ab-a^2}{ab-a^2+b^2}$ (need $b>a$).

Then $\frac1k=1+\frac{b^2}{a(b-a)}$. With $t=b-a>0$: $\frac{b^2}{a t}=\frac{(a+t)^2}{at}=\frac at+2+\frac ta\ge4$. So $\frac1k\ge5$, $k\le\frac15$, with equality when $t=a$, i.e. $b=2a$.

**Answer: $\frac15$**

prompt: Let $f(x)=(x+3)^2+\dfrac94$ for $x\ge-3$. Compute the shortest possible distance between a point on the graph of $f$ and a point on the graph of $f^{-1}$.

solutions.title: Reflect in $y=x$
solutions.body:
The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y=x$. Since $f(x)-x=x^2+5x+\frac{45}4>0$ for all $x$, the graph of $f$ lies entirely above the line $y=x$ and that of $f^{-1}$ entirely below it. A segment joining them crosses the line, so its length is at least the sum of the distances of its endpoints to the line, which is at least $2\cdot\min(\text{distance from graph of }f\text{ to line }y=x)$; and this is achieved by joining a point $(x,f(x))$ to its reflection $(f(x),x)$.

The distance between $(x,f(x))$ and $(f(x),x)$ is $\sqrt2\,|f(x)-x|=\sqrt2\left(x^2+5x+\frac{45}4\right)$, minimised at $x=-\frac52$ (allowed, since $-\frac52\ge-3$), where $x^2+5x+\frac{45}4=\frac{25}4-\frac{25}2+\frac{45}4=5$. So the minimum distance is $5\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $5\sqrt2$**
